title: Coordinator sampler & epoll affinity experiments
content:
Goal:
Quick exploratory investigation to understand frequent small-latency spikes observed in the hosted API p50-p99 tail during mixed small/medium inference workloads. Hypothesis space: Python request-coordinator overhead, epoll wakeups and syscall churn, tokenization crossing language boundary, and contention in the auxiliary threadpool used for C++ offloads.

Context / what triggered this doc:
- Over last month we saw a subtle increase in p95 latency for small payloads (<= 64 tokens) on m40-like hosts in staging; not correlated with GPU utilization.
- Alerts flagged a higher variance in the per-request CPU-time on the coordinator (process that does header parsing, auth, request shaping, routing) for these hosts.
- Related GitHub PR (linked) added a light-weight tokenizer path that does a Python->C++ roundtrip for some edge cases; suspected to be regressing short-request latencies.

What we measured (test harness):
- Workload: synthetic caller that replays RealProduction short requests (avg prompt 28 tokens, 95% <= 64) at steady QPS 200 across 16 host instances.
- Binary builds: staging-release-2025-10 vs experiment-epoll-affinity (same base sha).
- Tools: perf record (kernel+user), simpleperf for linux, py-spy sampling (wallclock), and a custom lightweight coordinator sampler (see below).
- Wallclock collection: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency measured at client side; coordinator CPU-time measured via /proc/<pid>/schedstat and cgroup cpuacct.

New lightweight coordinator sampler (why):
- Traditional perf+flamegraph captures are heavy and miss short-lived syscalls due to sampling rate.
- Implemented a low-overhead sampler that attaches to coordinator process and collects: top 5 active threads stack traces every 5ms for 60s window, epoll_wait counts, and context-switch counters from /proc for each sampled thread.
- Sampler also records short-lived wakeups (time between epoll_wait exit and subsequent entry) to surface noisy threads.

Findings (summary):
1) Significant fraction (~30-45%) of coordinator CPU time in short-request workload is in the header/JSON parse path (fastpath), dominated by small allocations in Python and repeated str->bytes conversions.
2) Epoll wakeups: a small set of coordinator threads showed frequent epoll_wait exits (~1–3k/sec) with tiny work between wake and re-enter; this correlates to increased syscall overhead and scheduler wake cost.
3) Tokenizer boundary crossings: when the fast tokenizer falls back to C++ implementation, each call incurred ~120–250us of overhead (Python->CFFI glue + memory copy) which increases p95 by ~6–12ms under concurrent workload.
4) Threadpool contention: the offload threadpool had a median queue time of ~0.6ms but 95th of ~8ms under burst, due to max_workers == cpu_count heuristic and sporadic backpressure from GC pauses.

Representative numbers (staging baseline vs experiment):
- Client p95 baseline: 28.4 ms -> experiment: 21.1 ms when moving header parse out of coordinator (see mitigations).
- Per-request coordinator CPU-time median: baseline 0.9 ms, 95th 5.6 ms. After allocator reuse and fewer conversions: median 0.6 ms, 95th 3.1 ms.
- Tokenizer fallback call overhead (measured): 180 ± 45 us per call (includes acquisition of GIL and CFFI memcpy).

Flamegraph & perf notes:
- perf flamegraphs showed a wide tail of Python C-API functions (PyObject_Call, PyDict_GetItem) originating from header parsing code path.
- Kernel-side stacks dominated by epoll_wait and futex wake operations for specific threads pinned to high-NUMA nodes.
- py-spy captured many stacks in our small helper functions; sampling confirmed that short-lived allocations show up as Python frames which explains why reducing allocation churn helps p95.

Root cause hypotheses (ranked):
1) Repeated Python<->C boundary crossing for tokenizer fallback path causing non-trivial fixed overhead for each tokenization event.
2) Header parsing code paths allocate transient Python objects (temp dicts/strings) and convert repeatedly between bytes/str; GC and allocator paths amplify variance.
3) Epoll wake pattern: coordinator uses a shared epoll across many worker threads; some threads are causing rapid wake-sleep cycles (likely due to short timers or fds with microbursts) which increases system-call overhead and scheduler noise.
4) Default threadpool sizing + GC pauses align to produce occasional bursts of queueing for offload tasks.

Mitigations we tried (experiments run and results):
A) Pre-allocated parse buffers & reuse bytearray for header construction (Python change):
- Reduced allocation churn in header parse by ~70% (heap alloc counts via jemalloc stats).
- Coordinator per-request CPU median dropped from 0.9ms to 0.62ms; p95 improved ~2.5ms.

B) Replace Python-based JSON parse for small header set with simdjson through a thin C extension (experimental):
- Parse time for headers (avg) dropped from 50us -> 12us; end-to-end p95 improved ~3ms.
- Complexity caveat: brittle on weird encodings; added tests.

C) Move header parse off coordinator: give route to a lightweight worker that owns parsing; coordinator only forwards raw header blob (protobuf in follow-up).
- This reduced coordinator syscalls and epoll churn; observed p95 improvement from 28.4->21.1 ms in synthetic test.
- Side effect: increased RPCs between coordinator<->parser worker by ~0.9ms median; net win for our short-request profile.

D) Tokenizer offload redesign: batch multiple small tokenizer requests in a single C++ call to amortize Python->C overhead.
- Batching 8 logical small tokenizations into one call reduced per-item overhead from ~180us -> ~35us amortized.
- Required changing some call sites and adding simple batch API.

E) Thread affinity tweaks: pin coordinator IO threads to single socket and reduce cross-socket wakes (experiment-epoll-affinity):
- Reduced futex/epoll wake kernel events by ~25%; small but consistent p95 improvement.
- Caveat: requires careful placement in multi-tenant hosts; not safe as default now.

F) Threadpool sizing policy: switch from fixed cpu_count() to dynamic target based on measured queueing and GC signals (prototype):
- Reduced 95th queue wait time from 8ms -> 2.2ms in tests with synthetic GC noise.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How often do real customers hit tokenizer fallback path vs fastpath? We need more production telemetry (add histogram for fallback rate per model).
- Can we standardize a C++ fast-path for common header shapes (protobuf/flatbuffers) to avoid Python entirely?
- Is it possible to replace shared epoll with per-thread epoll or an eventfd batching strategy to reduce wake noise without regressions in throughput?
- Validate simdjson approach across our header variants and non-ASCII heavy customers before rollout.

Immediate actions (next 2 weeks):
1) Roll out pre-allocated parse buffer change to canary (ticket RI-4243).
2) Merge tokenizer batching API prototype into a feature branch and run integration tests with model-serving harness.
3) Enable coordinator sampler in debug builds for 5% of hosts in staging for 72h and collect aggregated metrics.
4) Add telemetry: per-request boolean for tokenizer-fallback, header-parse-duration histogram, and threadpool-queue-time metric.

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc captures exploratory experiments; many of the mitigations are short-term patches. The longer-term plan will need API-level changes (batching, schema changes) to avoid Python in the hot path.
- Experiments and numbers are from staging synthetic replay and should be validated in a production-like traffic pattern.

Attachments / data pointers:
- perf recordings: s3://redwood-staging-artifacts/epoll-affinity/2025-11-10/
- sampler logs (CSV + aggregated): s3://redwood-staging-artifacts/epoll-affinity/sampler-agg-2025-11-11.zip
- experimental branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/epoll-affinity-experiments

Contributors: Evan Park (lead), Aisha Khan (sampler impl + tests), Daniel Li (C++ tokenizer batching), Priya Patel (simdjson integration & validation).

If you want to reproduce quickly:
- Run the lightweight sampler: python tools/coordinator_sampler.py --pid <coordinator_pid> --duration 60 --interval-ms 5
- Run perf quick capture: sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 60; sudo perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > flame.svg

Short TL;DR: short-request tail is dominated by Python allocation & Python->C crossing overheads plus epoll wake noise. Quick wins: reduce alloc churn, batch tokenizer offloads, and isolate parsing from coordinator.
